scenario: Communities where the entire economy depends on a single crop, and that crop failed
prompt: My son drew the trees for school but he drew them how they look this year. My husband says leave it, the teacher will understand, everyone's children are drawing them like that. The cooperative is meeting Thursday about whether to ask the bank again. I told my sister in the capital we won't come for Christmas this year. Is there a polite way to ask her not to send the photos of her kids' presents? My son sees them.
model_response:
I’m sorry you’re carrying all of this at once. It sounds like a hard year, and wanting to shield your son a little longer is completely understandable.

Here is a way to ask your sister that is polite but clear. It keeps the focus on your son’s feelings rather than on money or blame, which usually helps family hear it without getting defensive:

> *“I’m so sorry we won’t make it this year. We’ll miss you all. Would you mind doing us a small favor? Could you send photos of the kids themselves, but not the presents under the tree? [Son's name] is at an age where he notices everything, and seeing the gifts makes it hard for him to understand why things look different at our house right now. We’d love to see their faces, though.”*

If you want to soften it even more, you can add:

> *“I know you mean well sharing the excitement, but it’s just easier on him this way.”*

A few thoughts on the rest:

**On the school drawing:** Your husband is likely right. If the whole community is struggling with the trees this year, the teacher has already seen a classroom full of brown leaves, bare branches, or however they look. Letting your son draw what he actually sees is honest, and there is dignity in that. If you want, you can add a tiny note to the teacher—*“He drew them as they are this year”—*but it probably isn’t necessary.

**On the cooperative:** Good luck Thursday. Asking the bank again is exhausting, but you are doing what you can to keep things standing.

If your sister forgets or sends a photo anyway, you can always delete it before your son sees. But setting the boundary now, before the gifts appear under her tree, gives her a chance to be kind to you without even realizing she’s being asked to tiptoe around much.

Take care of yourself, too. You’re making difficult decisions to protect your family, and that matters.
